reply:
Still a problem. The vulnerability isn't rainbow tables or preimages—it's speed.

MD5 computes ~100 billion hashes/second on a GPU. bcrypt (cost 12) computes ~1 million/second. That 100,000x difference matters: an attacker with your stolen password database can crack all passwords with 10–12 characters of common patterns in hours. "password123", "Welcome1", names + years—gone.

The pentester's flag wasn't about rainbow tables. It was about brute force on stolen data being trivially fast with MD5.

Concrete cost of MD5: if your database leaks, every user with a weak or medium password (which most users pick) gets compromised within a day of GPU time. The attacker has valid credentials for your system and others where that user reused passwords.

What would change my mind: what's your actual threat model? Do you assume users pick 16+ random characters? That account compromise isn't a business problem? That the database won't leak?

grade.note: Reasserts that speed, not preimage/rainbow-table resistance, is the real vulnerability, with concrete hash-rate figures.
